concept.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory
concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

concept.lean_guess: Given an n-player game G with strategy sets S_1, ..., S_n. Define the simplex Delta = {(p_1, ..., p_n) : p_i in Delta(S_i), sum p_i = 1}. Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.

concept.title: Matroid Minors and the Graph Theorem: Robertson-Seymour for Matroids
concept.concept_description: The Robertson-Seymour theorem states that the set of finite graphs is well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation: any infinite sequence of graphs contains two where one is a minor of the other. This implies that any minor-closed graph property is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. Conjecture: the same theorem holds for representable matroids over any finite field. Specifically, for any finite field F_q, the set of F_q-representable matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation. This would generalize the Robertson-Seymour theorem from graphs (F_2-representable matroids) to all finite fields. The conjecture is known to fail for general matroids (by the existence of infinite antichains of non-representable matroids), but for F_q-representable matroids with q <= 3, it is open. Conjecture: for F_3 (ternary matroids), the set of excluded minors for representability is finite. The current known excluded minors for F_3 are: the Fano matroid F_7, its dual F_7*, and the non-Pappus matroid. Test: enumerate ternary matroids of rank 3 on 9 elements, verify that all but the known excluded minors are F_3-representable. Impact: Robertson-Seymour for matroids would unify graph minor theory and matroid theory under a single well-quasi-ordering theorem.

concept.lean_guess: Define matroid minor: M' is a minor of M if M' can be obtained from M by a sequence of deletions and contractions. The Robertson-Seymour theorem for graphs: for any infinite sequence G_1, G_2, ..., there exist i < j such that G_i is a minor of G_j. Conjecture: the same holds for F_q-representable matroids. For q=2 (graphs): this is Robertson-Seymour. For q=3: this is open. Known result: the set of excluded minors for F_3-representability is {F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus}. The conjecture would follow from: (1) F_3-representable matroids are well-quasi-ordered under the minor relation, and (2) any minor-closed class of F_3-representable matroids has finitely many excluded minors. Step (1) requires showing that F_3-representable matroids contain no infinite antichain. The known antichains (uniform matroids U_{2,n} for n >= 4) are NOT F_3-representable for large n. Step (2) follows from (1) by the same argument as Robertson-Seymour. Test: enumerate all rank-3 matroids on 9 elements (there are ~100), check F_3-representability, verify that excluded minors are exactly F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus.

concept.title: The Fourier Analysis of Collatz: Spectral Gaps in the 3n+1 Map
concept.concept_description: The Collatz map T: N -> N defined by T(n) = n/2 if n even, 3n+1 if n odd, is conjectured to always reach 1. The Collatz conjecture is equivalent to: the orbit of every n under T eventually reaches the cycle {1, 4, 2, 1}. Define the Collatz Fourier transform: F_T(omega) = sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n} for N large. Conjecture: F_T has a spectral gap: |F_T(omega)| < C for all irrational omega, where C < sqrt(N). This would mean that the Collatz map does not concentrate energy at any irrational frequency — it is 'mixing' in the Fourier sense. Moreover, the spectral gap is related to the convergence rate: the wider the gap, the faster the orbit reaches 1. Conjecture: for the orbit of n, the number of steps to reach 1 is O(log(n)), which is equivalent to F_T having a spectral gap of width Omega(1/log(n)). Test: compute F_T for n up to 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with the spectral gaps of related maps (5n+1, 7n+1) which do NOT always converge. Impact: the Collatz conjecture is a spectral gap problem. Convergence to 1 means the Fourier transform has no resonances at irrational frequencies.

concept.lean_guess: Define F_T(omega) = (1/N) * sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n}. For rational omega = p/q: F_T(p/q) measures the correlation between T(n)/n and the frequency p/q. For T(n) = n/2 (even case) or T(n) = (3n+1)/2 (odd case, accelerating), the ratio T(n)/n is either 1/2 or approximately 3/2 + 1/(2n). The spectral gap of F_T is: gap = inf_{|omega|>0} |F_T(omega)| / F_T(0). For a mixing map, F_T(omega) -> 0 as N -> infinity for irrational omega. This is the von Neumann ergodic theorem for the 3n+1 map. If the 3n+1 map is mixing (which is conjectured but not known), then F_T has a spectral gap. The connection to Collatz convergence: if T is mixing, then the orbit of n visits the set {1} with positive density, which implies it eventually reaches 1. The spectral gap width determines the convergence rate: a gap of width delta gives convergence in O(log(n)/delta) steps. Test: compute F_T(omega) for N = 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with 5n+1 (which has orbits that may diverge) and n+1 (which converges in n steps).

concept.title: The Arithmetic of Games: Surreal Numbers as Number Fields
concept.concept_description: Conway's surreal numbers No form a proper class containing all real numbers, all ordinal numbers, and all infinitesimals. Every real number r has a surreal representation r = {r - 1 | r + 1}. Every ordinal alpha has a surreal representation alpha = {alpha |}. Every infinitesimal epsilon = {0 | 1, 1/2, 1/4, ...}. The surreal numbers form a field (in fact, a real-closed field). Conjecture: the subfield of surreals born by day omega (the set of surreals with finite birthdays) is isomorphic to the field of real algebraic numbers extended with all dyadic rationals. More precisely: No_{omega} = Q[2^{-n} : n in N] (the rationals extended with all dyadic rationals). The subfield born by day omega^2 contains all real numbers that are algebraic over the dyadic rationals, plus all infinitesimals that are algebraic over the reals. Conjecture: No_{omega^2} = R(x) where x is the smallest positive infinitesimal. Test: compute the field structure of surreals born by day omega and verify the isomorphism with the dyadic rationals. Impact: the surreal number hierarchy encodes the constructive hierarchy of real number fields — each birthday level adds exactly the algebraic closures needed.

import Mathlib.SetTheory.Surreal.Dyadic

/-!
# Dyadic rationals embed in the surreal numbers

This file closes the injectivity gap left in the dyadic-surreal construction. It proves that
`Surreal.dyadicMap`, from the localization `ℤ[1/2]` to surreal numbers, is injective. Consequently
its range is additively equivalent to the dyadic rationals, and equality of two standard dyadic
fractions is characterized by cross multiplication.
-/

open SetTheory

namespace SetTheory.PGame

/-
The canonical game tree for `2⁻ⁿ` has birthday exactly `n + 1`. Thus every canonical dyadic
unit is born before day omega, while their birthdays are unbounded among the finite ordinals.
-/
@[simp] theorem birthday_powHalf (n : ℕ) : birthday (powHalf n) = n + 1 := by
  induction n <;> simp_all +decide [ powHalf ];
  simp +decide [ *, PGame.birthday ];
  exact Order.one_le_iff_pos.mpr ( Ordinal.succ_pos _ )

end SetTheory.PGame

namespace Surreal

/-
Every explicitly constructed inverse power of two is strictly positive as a surreal number.
-/
theorem powHalf_pos (n : ℕ) : 0 < powHalf n := by
  convert SetTheory.PGame.powHalf_pos n using 1

/-
An integer multiple of an inverse power of two vanishes only when the integer vanishes.
-/
theorem zsmul_powHalf_eq_zero_iff (m : ℤ) (n : ℕ) :
    m • powHalf n = 0 ↔ m = 0 := by
  simp +zetaDelta at *
  exact fun h => absurd h (powHalf_pos n |> ne_of_gt)

/-
The canonical inverse powers of two form a strictly decreasing sequence.
-/
theorem powHalf_strictAnti : StrictAnti powHalf := by
  refine' strictAnti_nat_of_succ_lt _;
  convert PGame.powHalf_succ_lt_powHalf using 1

/-
Two canonical inverse powers of two are equal precisely when their exponents agree.
-/
@[simp] theorem powHalf_injective_eq (m n : ℕ) : powHalf m = powHalf n ↔ m = n := by
  exact ⟨ fun h => StrictAnti.injective powHalf_strictAnti h, fun h => h ▸ rfl ⟩

/-
The canonical additive map from dyadic rationals `ℤ[1/2]` into the surreals is injective.
-/
theorem dyadicMap_injective : Function.Injective dyadicMap := by
  intro x y hxy;
  by_contra hxy';
  obtain ⟨m, n, hm⟩ : ∃ m n : ℤ, ∃ k : ℕ, x = IsLocalization.mk' (Localization.Away 2) m (Submonoid.pow 2 k) ∧ y = IsLocalization.mk' (Localization.Away 2) n (Submonoid.pow 2 k) := by
    obtain ⟨ m, s, hm ⟩ := IsLocalization.mk'_surjective ( Submonoid.powers ( 2 : ℤ ) ) x
    obtain ⟨ n, t, hn ⟩ := IsLocalization.mk'_surjective ( Submonoid.powers ( 2 : ℤ ) ) y;
    obtain ⟨ k₁, hk₁ ⟩ := m.2.2
    obtain ⟨ k₂, hk₂ ⟩ := n.2.2
    use m.1 * 2 ^ k₂, n.1 * 2 ^ k₁, k₁ + k₂;
    constructor <;> rw [ IsLocalization.eq ];
    · simp +decide [← hk₁, pow_add, mul_comm, mul_left_comm];
    · simp_all +decide [pow_add, mul_comm, mul_left_comm];
  obtain ⟨ k, rfl, rfl ⟩ := hm; simp_all +decide;
  exact absurd ( hxy.resolve_left ( by aesop ) ) ( ne_of_gt ( powHalf_pos k ) )

/-- The dyadic rationals are equivalent to the dyadic surreal numbers. The equivalence is
canonical: it is induced by `dyadicMap`. -/
noncomputable def dyadicEquiv : Localization.Away (2 : ℤ) ≃ dyadic :=
  Equiv.ofInjective dyadicMap dyadicMap_injective

@[simp]
theorem dyadicEquiv_apply (x : Localization.Away (2 : ℤ)) :
    (dyadicEquiv x : Surreal) = dyadicMap x := by
  rfl

/-
Equality of dyadic surreal values is exactly equality of the corresponding cross products.
-/
theorem zsmul_powHalf_eq_iff_cross_mul (m₁ m₂ : ℤ) (n₁ n₂ : ℕ) :
    m₁ • powHalf n₁ = m₂ • powHalf n₂ ↔
      m₁ * (2 : ℤ) ^ n₂ = m₂ * (2 : ℤ) ^ n₁ := by
  convert dyadicMap_injective.eq_iff using 1;
  rotate_left;
  rotate_left;
  exact Localization.mk m₁ ( Submonoid.pow 2 n₁ );
  exact Localization.mk m₂ ( Submonoid.pow 2 n₂ );
  simp +decide [ dyadicMap ];
  congr! 1;
  · erw [ Localization.liftOn_mk ] ; aesop;
  · erw [ Localization.liftOn_mk ] ; aesop;
  · rw [ Localization.mk_eq_mk_iff ];
    simp +decide [ Localization.r_iff_exists, Submonoid.pow ];
    exact ⟨ fun h => ⟨ 2 ^ n₂, ⟨ n₂, rfl ⟩, Or.inl <| by linarith ⟩, fun ⟨ a, ha, ha' ⟩ => by cases ha' <;> simp_all +decide [ mul_comm, Submonoid.mem_powers_iff ] ⟩

/-
The canonical surreal representatives `m / 2^n` are unique up to the usual
cross-multiplication relation.
-/
theorem dyadicMap_mk'_eq_iff (m₁ m₂ : ℤ) (n₁ n₂ : ℕ) :
    dyadicMap (IsLocalization.mk' (Localization.Away (2 : ℤ)) m₁ (Submonoid.pow 2 n₁)) =
      dyadicMap (IsLocalization.mk' (Localization.Away (2 : ℤ)) m₂ (Submonoid.pow 2 n₂)) ↔
        m₁ * (2 : ℤ) ^ n₂ = m₂ * (2 : ℤ) ^ n₁ := by
  convert zsmul_powHalf_eq_iff_cross_mul m₁ m₂ n₁ n₂ using 1;
  simp +decide only [dyadicMap_apply_pow];
  convert Iff.rfl

end Surreal

namespace DyadicLocalization

/-
The localization `ℤ[1/2]` is not a field: three has no multiplicative inverse. This pinpoints a
basic obstruction in calling the finite-birthday surreals a *subfield*: the finite-birthday
surreals are dyadic, but division by `3` leaves that class.
-/
theorem three_has_no_inverse :
    ¬ ∃ x : Localization.Away (2 : ℤ), (3 : Localization.Away (2 : ℤ)) * x = 1 := by
  by_contra h_contra;
  obtain ⟨ x, hx ⟩ := h_contra
  have h_eq : 3 * (3 * x) = 3 := by
    rw [ hx, mul_one ];
  obtain ⟨ y, hy ⟩ := IsLocalization.mk'_surjective ( Submonoid.powers 2 : Submonoid ℤ ) x;
  simp_all +decide [mul_comm];
  have h_eq : y.1 * 3 = y.2.val := by
    have h_eq : IsLocalization.mk' (Localization.Away (2 : ℤ)) (y.1 * 3) y.2 = 1 := by
      convert hx using 1;
      rw [ ← hy, mul_comm ];
      rw [ mul_comm, IsLocalization.mk'_eq_iff_eq_mul ];
      rw [ mul_right_comm, IsLocalization.mk'_spec ];
      norm_num [ Algebra.smul_def ];
    rw [ IsLocalization.mk'_eq_iff_eq_mul ] at h_eq;
    erw [ one_mul ] at h_eq;
    erw [ IsLocalization.eq_iff_exists ( Submonoid.powers ( 2 : ℤ ) ) ] at h_eq;
    exact mul_left_cancel₀ ( show ( h_eq.choose : ℤ ) ≠ 0 from by obtain ⟨ k, hk ⟩ := h_eq.choose.2; aesop ) h_eq.choose_spec;
  rcases y with ⟨ y₁, y₂ ⟩;
  obtain ⟨ k, hk ⟩ := y₂.2;
  replace hk := congr_arg ( · % 3 ) hk ; norm_num [ ← h_eq, Int.mul_emod ] at hk;
  norm_cast at hk ; rcases Nat.even_or_odd' k with ⟨ k, rfl | rfl ⟩ <;> norm_num [ Nat.pow_add, Nat.pow_mul, Nat.mul_mod, Nat.pow_mod ] at hk;
  · bv_omega;
  · replace h_eq := congr_arg ( · % 3 ) h_eq ; norm_num [ Int.mul_emod, hk.symm ] at h_eq

end DyadicLocalization

# Computational evidence

The relevant finite computations are symbolic rather than floating-point approximations. For the canonical dyadic surreal `powHalf n`, the formal recurrence is

| `n` | surreal value | left options | right options | birthday |
|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| 0 | `1` | `{0}` | empty | 1 |
| 1 | `1/2` | `{0}` | `{1}` | 2 |
| 2 | `1/4` | `{0}` | `{1/2}` | 3 |
| 3 | `1/8` | `{0}` | `{1/4}` | 4 |
| 4 | `1/16` | `{0}` | `{1/8}` | 5 |
| 5 | `1/32` | `{0}` | `{1/16}` | 6 |

These instances suggest, and the Lean development proves for every natural `n`, that the birthday is `n + 1` and that the values form a strictly decreasing positive sequence.

For uniqueness, sample cross-product checks agree with the proved criterion:

* `1/2 = 2/4` because `1·4 = 2·2`.
* `3/8 = 6/16` because `3·16 = 6·8`.
* `1/2 ≠ 3/4` because `1·4 ≠ 3·2`.
* `-3/8 = -6/16` because `(-3)·16 = (-6)·8`.

A counterexample hunt against the prompt's “subfield” wording finds the immediate obstruction `1/3`: if `m/2ⁿ` were an inverse of `3`, then `3m = 2ⁿ`, impossible since no power of two is divisible by three. This obstruction is also proved in Lean as `DyadicLocalization.three_has_no_inverse`.

No OEIS search is relevant: the sequences of values `2⁻ⁿ` and birthdays `n+1` are elementary closed-form sequences, and no combinatorial sequence identification is needed for the theorem.

# Future directions

## What was established

`Algebra/SurrealDyadic.lean` formalizes the canonical dyadic part of the surreal hierarchy.

* The canonical pre-game for `2⁻ⁿ` has birthday exactly `n + 1`.
* The surreal values `2⁻ⁿ` are positive and strictly decrease with `n`.
* An integer multiple `m · 2⁻ⁿ` is zero exactly when `m = 0`.
* The existing canonical additive map `ℤ[1/2] → No` is injective. Hence its image, the dyadic surreal numbers, is canonically equivalent as a type to `ℤ[1/2]`.
* Equality of canonical values `m₁/2ⁿ¹` and `m₂/2ⁿ²` is equivalent to the cross-product identity
  `m₁ 2ⁿ² = m₂ 2ⁿ¹`.
* `3` has no inverse in `ℤ[1/2]`, so the dyadic rationals are not a field.

The last point corrects an important issue in the research prompt: the finite-birthday surreal numbers are expected to form the dyadic **subring**, not a subfield. Closing under inverses would already require `1/3`, which is not dyadic and is not born on a finite day.

## Next formal targets

1. **Classify every finite-birthday surreal.** Prove both directions of the precise statement: a surreal has a representative of finite birthday iff it lies in `Surreal.dyadic`. The forward direction should induct on a numeric pre-game's birthday and identify the simplest dyadic strictly between its finite sets of dyadic options. This requires a formal “simplest dyadic in an interval” theorem.

2. **Upgrade the image equivalence algebraically.** The current Mathlib surreal development supplies addition but not a full ring structure on `Surreal`; consequently the proved equivalence is a plain equivalence induced by an injective additive map. Once surreal multiplication and its laws are available, prove that `dyadicMap` is multiplicative and package its range as an ordered subring isomorphic to `ℤ[1/2]`.

3. **Canonical birthday formula for general dyadics.** For a reduced noninteger dyadic `m/2ⁿ` with odd `m`, determine and prove the exact birthday. The answer depends on the integer part as well as the denominator exponent; the theorem for `2⁻ⁿ` in this project is the basic case.

4. **Separate birthday cutoffs from algebraic closure.** Birthday-bounded classes need not be subfields or even subrings at a fixed bound, since arithmetic can increase birthdays. Future statements should explicitly distinguish (a) numbers born before an ordinal, (b) the ring generated by those numbers, and (c) the field generated by them.

5. **Reassess the proposed `No_{ω²} = ℝ(x)` claim.** Before formalization, specify whether the cutoff is `< ω²` and what closure operation is intended. Also, there is no smallest positive surreal infinitesimal: if `x > 0` is infinitesimal, then `x/2` is a smaller positive infinitesimal once field arithmetic is available. Thus the phrase “the smallest positive infinitesimal” must be replaced, for example by the particular monomial `ω⁻¹`; even then equality with `ℝ(ω⁻¹)` requires substantial correction because bounded-birthday classes and generated rational-function fields are different constructions.

# The Arithmetic of Games: How Finite Surreal Numbers Become Dyadic

## A number born from a choice

Most number systems begin with objects and then add rules. The surreal numbers reverse that order. A surreal number is born from a choice between two collections of earlier numbers. It is written

$$
\{L\mid R\},
$$

where every member of the left set $L$ is smaller than every member of the right set $R$. The new number is the simplest number lying strictly between those options. This construction turns arithmetic into a family tree: each number has a birthday recording the stage at which its description first becomes available.

The first day is almost empty. With no options on either side, one obtains

$$
0=\{\,\mid\,\}.
$$

Once zero exists, the next stage produces

$$
1=\{0\mid\},\qquad -1=\{\mid 0\}.
$$

Then the gap between $0$ and $1$ yields

$$
\frac12=\{0\mid 1\}.
$$

The next rounds create halves of halves, odd numerators between neighboring fractions, and ever larger integers. This simple game of choosing a left and a right boundary eventually generates an enormous ordered number system containing the familiar real numbers, ordinal numbers, infinitely large quantities, and infinitesimals.

But the finite opening of this universe has a strikingly rigid arithmetic shape. It is governed not by arbitrary fractions, but by the **dyadic rationals**: numbers of the form

$$
\frac{m}{2^n},
$$

where $m$ is an integer and $n$ is a nonnegative integer. The arithmetic developed here explains why the powers of two are not an accident, why their canonical surreal representatives are distinct, and why this finite-birthday world is a ring rather than a field.

## The binary staircase

Begin with the canonical game for $1$ and repeatedly take the simplest number between $0$ and the preceding value. This creates

$$
1,\quad \frac12,\quad \frac14,\quad \frac18,\quad \ldots.
$$

The key birthday theorem says that the canonical representative of $2^{-n}$ has birthday exactly $n+1$. Thus $1=2^0$ appears at birthday $1$, $1/2$ at birthday $2$, $1/4$ at birthday $3$, and so on.

This result says two things at once. First, every inverse power of two appears after finitely many stages. Second, no fixed finite stage contains them all: their birthdays are unbounded among the natural numbers. The approach to zero is therefore also a journey deeper into the construction.

These values behave exactly as their ordinary fractional notation suggests. Every $2^{-n}$ is positive, and the sequence is strictly decreasing:

$$
2^{-(n+1)}<2^{-n}.
$$

Consequently, two canonical inverse powers of two are equal if and only if their exponents agree. The hierarchy does not accidentally collapse $1/4$ and $1/8$, for example; order keeps every rung of the binary staircase separate.

There is another essential cancellation fact. If $m$ is an integer, then

$$
m\,2^{-n}=0
$$

holds if and only if $m=0$. A nonzero integer cannot annihilate a positive inverse power of two. This elementary-looking statement is the hinge on which uniqueness turns.

## Fractions that cannot disguise themselves

A dyadic number can have more than one written form. For instance,

$$
\frac12=\frac24=\frac48.
$$

So the right uniqueness statement cannot require identical numerators and denominators. Instead, it uses the familiar rule of cross multiplication.

For integers $m_1,m_2$ and nonnegative integers $n_1,n_2$, the corresponding surreal dyadics satisfy

$$
m_1 2^{-n_1}=m_2 2^{-n_2}
$$

if and only if

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

This is the **Cross-Multiplication Theorem for Dyadic Surreals**. It provides a complete test for equality using integer arithmetic alone. As an example,

$$
\frac{6}{2^4}=\frac{3}{2^3}
$$

because $6\cdot 2^3=3\cdot 2^4=48$. By contrast,

$$
\frac{5}{2^3}\ne\frac{3}{2^2}
$$

because $5\cdot 2^2=20$ while $3\cdot 2^3=24$.

This criterion proves that the canonical map from the localized ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ into the surreal numbers is injective. Here $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ means the integers with powers of two made invertible; concretely, it is precisely the set of fractions $m/2^n$. Injectivity means that no two genuinely different dyadic rationals become the same surreal number. The image is therefore a faithful copy of dyadic arithmetic inside the surreal universe.

There is a practical lesson here. Equality in a recursively generated world may look like a question about game trees, but for this entire family it reduces to a single multiplication test in the integers. The elaborate genealogy of a number and its ordinary arithmetic value agree perfectly.

## A ring, not a field

It is tempting to call every rich collection of numbers a field. The dyadic rationals are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication:

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
 =\frac{a2^n+b2^m}{2^{m+n}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}\frac{b}{2^n}=\frac{ab}{2^{m+n}}.
$$

They also contain $0$ and $1$. These properties make them a commutative ring. Yet division exposes a boundary. The number $3$ has no multiplicative inverse in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some dyadic $m/2^n$ were an inverse of $3$. Then

$$
3\frac{m}{2^n}=1,
$$

so

$$
3m=2^n.
$$

The left side is divisible by $3$, whereas no power of $2$ is divisible by $3$. This is impossible. Hence $1/3$ is not dyadic.

This obstruction corrects a subtle but important misconception about birthdays. The numbers born at finite stages are naturally associated with the dyadic **subring**, not a subfield. Closing that collection under multiplicative inverses would immediately force the inclusion of $1/3$, which does not have a finite birthday in the canonical surreal hierarchy.

The distinction matters far beyond terminology. A birthday cutoff describes when objects are constructed. A ring closure describes which objects arithmetic operations generate. A field closure additionally demands every nonzero inverse. These are different processes, and they need not preserve the same boundary.

## Why powers of two rule the finite days

The appearance of dyadics reflects a universal fact about repeatedly selecting simplest midpoints. Given neighboring dyadic boundaries, the simplest point inserted between them refines the denominator by a factor of two. Binary subdivision is built into the construction:

$$
0,1
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
0,\frac12,1
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,1.
$$

This is the same geometry behind binary search, bisection algorithms, digital fixed-point arithmetic, and subdivision meshes in computer graphics. A finite binary word records a finite route through successive left-right choices. Correspondingly, a dyadic fraction is exactly a rational number with a terminating binary expansion.

For example,

$$
\frac{13}{16}=0.1101_2.
$$

Its denominator records four levels of binary resolution. Surreal birthdays add a genealogical interpretation: denominator depth measures part of the history required to isolate the number, though for general dyadics the exact birthday also depends on the integer part and reduction of the fraction.

This makes dyadic surreals useful as a conceptual bridge. In numerical computation, dyadic fractions are the exactly representable finite binary values. In harmonic analysis, dyadic intervals organize functions by scale. In combinatorial game theory, birthdays organize numbers by constructive complexity. The same powers of two describe precision, scale, and ancestry.

## The horizon at day $\omega$

All finite birthdays lie before the first infinite ordinal $\omega$. The sequence $2^{-n}$ demonstrates what happens near that horizon: each term is born finitely, but there is no final finite day on which the entire sequence appears. The union of all finite stages contains every dyadic fraction, while remaining arithmetically incomplete as a field.

That observation prevents an easy but false leap from “all finite constructions” to “a closed number field.” The finite-birthday collection can support addition and multiplication of dyadic values, yet inversion can leave it. In particular, $3$ is present, but $1/3$ is not.

The next classification challenge is to prove the converse in full generality: not only does every canonical dyadic arise at a finite birthday, but every surreal with a finite-birthday representative is dyadic. The natural strategy is to inspect the finite left and right option sets and identify the simplest dyadic lying between them. Such a theorem would convert the vivid binary picture into a complete characterization of the finite region.

Beyond that boundary, one must proceed carefully. There is no smallest positive infinitesimal: given a positive infinitesimal $x$, the number $x/2$ is smaller and still positive. Thus any theory built around “the smallest positive infinitesimal” must instead choose a specific distinguished infinitesimal, such as $\omega^{-1}$. Likewise, a birthday-bounded class should never be silently identified with the ring or field it generates.

## The moral of the game

The surreal numbers show how a vast arithmetic universe can grow from an austere rule: choose earlier values on the left and right, then create the simplest number between them. In the finite stages, this rule speaks binary. The canonical units $2^{-n}$ appear on precisely scheduled birthdays, remain positive and strictly ordered, and admit no unexpected additive collapse. Integer multiples of these units give a faithful copy of $\mathbb Z[1/2]$, with equality decided exactly by cross multiplication.

And the first obstruction is just as illuminating as the successes: $3$ has no dyadic inverse. The finite world is not deficient because of an accident in notation. Its limitation is structural. Birthdays measure construction, while field operations demand closure, and those two ideas diverge as soon as one asks for $1/3$.

That is the arithmetic of games in miniature: a family tree that becomes a number line, a binary genealogy that becomes a ring, and a missing inverse that marks the boundary between finite construction and the larger surreal cosmos.

# Finite-Birthday Surreal Numbers and the Dyadic Ring

**Aristotle**  
**July 18, 2026**

## Abstract

Surreal numbers are recursively generated from cuts between previously constructed numbers, and their birthdays measure the stages at which representatives become available. This paper isolates the canonical dyadic fragment of that hierarchy. We prove that the canonical surreal representative of $2^{-n}$ has birthday exactly $n+1$, that these representatives are positive and strictly decreasing, and that a multiple $m2^{-n}$ vanishes only for $m=0$. We then establish that the canonical map from the localization $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ into the surreal numbers is injective. As a consequence, equality of two canonical dyadic surreal values is equivalent to the integer cross-product identity

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

Finally, we prove that $3$ has no inverse in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Thus the finite-birthday layer is naturally associated with the dyadic subring, not a subfield. The results clarify the distinction among birthday cutoffs, algebraic closures, and fields generated by birthday-bounded classes, while providing exact algorithms for equality, normalization, arithmetic, and birthday computation for canonical inverse powers of two.

## 1. Introduction

The surreal numbers arise from a recursive construction in which a new number is specified by previously available left and right options. A form

$$
x=\{L\mid R\}
$$

is valid when every $\ell\in L$ is less than every $r\in R$; its value is the simplest surreal number strictly between all left and right options. Starting from the empty cut, this process creates $0$, then the integers $\pm1$, then fractions such as $1/2$, and eventually a proper class encompassing the real numbers, ordinals, infinitesimals, and infinitely large quantities.

The recursive stages are measured by **birthdays**. The birthday of a form is one greater than the supremum of the birthdays of its options, with the empty form assigned birthday $0$. Birthday therefore records constructive depth rather than ordinary magnitude. An enormous integer and a tiny positive fraction can both have finite birthdays, but their exact dates reflect different genealogies.

The finite stages have long suggested a binary pattern. Repeatedly choosing the simplest value between $0$ and a previously created positive value yields

$$
1,\frac12,\frac14,\frac18,\ldots.
$$

More generally, finite binary subdivision produces numbers $m/2^n$. These are the dyadic rationals, algebraically described as the localization $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ obtained from $\mathbb Z$ by inverting $2$.

This paper develops the exact arithmetic facts required to identify the canonical dyadic values faithfully inside the surreal numbers. The principal issue is injectivity: distinct elements of $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ must not collapse to the same surreal value. Once injectivity is known, equality reduces to cross multiplication, exactly as for ordinary fractions.

A second objective is corrective. The dyadic rationals are sometimes described informally as a field, or the finite-birthday surreals as a subfield. This is false. Although $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is a commutative ordered ring, it does not contain $1/3$. We give an elementary obstruction proving that $3$ has no multiplicative inverse. Therefore finite birthdays, ring generation, and field generation must be distinguished.

## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1. Surreal forms and birthdays

A **surreal form** is a pair $\{L\mid R\}$ of sets of earlier forms satisfying $\ell<r$ for every $\ell\in L$ and $r\in R$. Two different forms may represent the same surreal number. The birthday belongs to a form and is recursively defined by

$$
b\bigl(\{L\mid R\}\bigr)
=
\sup\{b(y)+1:y\in L\cup R\}.
$$

For finite game trees, this is simply one plus the maximum birthday among all options. In particular,

$$
0=\{\mid\},\qquad b(0)=0,
$$

and

$$
1=\{0\mid\},\qquad b(1)=1.
$$

The distinction between a form and its value is important. Our birthday statements concern canonical recursively defined forms, while arithmetic statements concern their surreal values.

### 2.2. Canonical inverse powers of two

Define canonical forms $h_n$ recursively by

$$
h_0=1,
\qquad
h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}.
$$

The value of $h_n$ is $2^{-n}$. Thus

$$
h_0=1,
\quad h_1=\frac12,
\quad h_2=\frac14,
\quad h_3=\frac18.
$$

The cut description expresses $h_{n+1}$ as the simplest surreal number strictly between $0$ and $h_n$.

### 2.3. Dyadic rationals as a localization

The **dyadic rationals** form the ring

$$
D=\mathbb Z[1/2]
 =\left\{\frac{m}{2^n}:m\in\mathbb Z,\ n\in\mathbb N\right\}.
$$

Two presentations represent the same element precisely when

$$
\frac{m_1}{2^{n_1}}=\frac{m_2}{2^{n_2}}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

Addition and multiplication are given by

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{a2^n+b2^m}{2^{m+n}},
$$

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{ab}{2^{m+n}}.
$$

A more economical addition algorithm first raises both values only to the common exponent $k=\max(m,n)$:

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{a2^{k-m}+b2^{k-n}}{2^k}.
$$

The canonical map into the surreal numbers is

$$
\iota:D\longrightarrow \mathbf{No},
\qquad
\iota\left(\frac{m}{2^n}\right)=m h_n=m2^{-n}.
$$

The central task is to show that this formula is independent of presentation and that $\iota$ is injective.

## 3. Birthday and order structure

### Theorem 3.1 (Exact birthday of a canonical dyadic unit)

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the canonical form $h_n$ representing $2^{-n}$ has birthday

$$
b(h_n)=n+1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The argument is induction on $n$. The base form $h_0=1=\{0\mid\}$ has birthday $1$. For the induction step, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$. Its options have birthdays $0$ and $n+1$, so the recursive birthday rule gives

$$
b(h_{n+1})=1+\max(0,n+1)=n+2.
$$

This is the required formula with $n$ replaced by $n+1$. $\square$

### Corollary 3.2 (Finite but unbounded birthdays)

Every canonical inverse power $2^{-n}$ has a finite-birthday representative, but their birthdays are unbounded among the finite ordinals.

**Proof sketch.** Finiteness follows from $b(h_n)=n+1$. Given any finite bound $N$, choosing $n\ge N$ yields $b(h_n)=n+1>N$. $\square$

### Theorem 3.3 (Positivity)

For every $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
0<h_n.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The base case $h_0=1$ is positive. Recursively, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$ is defined as a number strictly to the right of its left option $0$. Hence it is positive. $\square$

### Theorem 3.4 (Strict decrease)

The sequence $n\mapsto h_n$ is strictly decreasing. Equivalently,

$$
h_{n+1}<h_n
$$

for every $n$, and if $m<n$ then $h_n<h_m$.

**Proof sketch.** By construction, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$ lies strictly below its right option $h_n$. Iterating this adjacent inequality proves strict antitonicity. $\square$

### Corollary 3.5 (Distinct exponents give distinct units)

For $m,n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
h_m=h_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m=n.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Equality follows immediately when $m=n$. Conversely, a strictly decreasing sequence is injective, so equal values force equal indices. $\square$

These results exhibit a direct relation between genealogy and order. As birthday increases along this family, value decreases toward zero. The family has no least positive member because $h_{n+1}$ is always a smaller positive member than $h_n$.

## 4. Cancellation and faithful embedding

### Lemma 4.1 (No nontrivial integer annihilator)

For every $m\in\mathbb Z$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
mh_n=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m=0.
$$

**Proof sketch.** If $m=0$, the equality is immediate. Conversely, $h_n>0$, hence $h_n\ne0$. The ordered additive group of surreal numbers is torsion-free: a positive integer multiple of a positive value is positive, while a negative integer multiple is negative. Therefore a nonzero integer multiple of $h_n$ cannot vanish. $\square$

The next result is the main arithmetic statement.

### Theorem 4.2 (Injectivity of the canonical dyadic map)

The map

$$
\iota:\mathbb Z[1/2]\longrightarrow\mathbf{No},
\qquad
\iota(m/2^n)=mh_n,
$$

is injective.

**Proof sketch.** Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ and suppose $\iota(x)=\iota(y)$. Choose presentations

$$
x=\frac{a}{2^r},\qquad y=\frac{b}{2^s}.
$$

Raise both to the common denominator $2^{r+s}$:

$$
x=\frac{a2^s}{2^{r+s}},
\qquad
 y=\frac{b2^r}{2^{r+s}}.
$$

Their surreal images are therefore integer multiples of the same positive unit $h_{r+s}$. Equality gives

$$
(a2^s-b2^r)h_{r+s}=0.
$$

By Lemma 4.1, $a2^s-b2^r=0$. Hence the two fractions are equal in the localization, so $x=y$. $\square$

### Corollary 4.3 (Canonical equivalence with the dyadic image)

The dyadic rational ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is in canonical bijection with its image in the surreal numbers.

**Proof sketch.** Any map is surjective onto its image. Combining this fact with Theorem 4.2 gives a bijection. $\square$

This equivalence is an exact identification at the level of values: each dyadic rational has one surreal value, and each surreal value in the image has one dyadic rational antecedent. The theorem does not claim that all surreal numbers are dyadic, nor by itself classify every finite-birthday form.

## 5. Equality by cross multiplication

### Theorem 5.1 (Cross-Multiplication Theorem)

For all $m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z$ and $n_1,n_2\in\mathbb N$,

$$
m_1h_{n_1}=m_2h_{n_2}
$$

if and only if

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Regard the two sides as the images under $\iota$ of $m_1/2^{n_1}$ and $m_2/2^{n_2}$. Injectivity of $\iota$ converts equality of surreal values into equality in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Equality of localized fractions is exactly the displayed cross-product identity. Conversely, the cross-product identity proves equality of fractions, and applying $\iota$ gives equality of their surreal values. $\square$

### Example 5.2

The values $6h_4$ and $3h_3$ are equal because

$$
6\cdot2^3=48=3\cdot2^4.
$$

Both represent $3/8$.

### Example 5.3

The values $5h_3$ and $3h_2$ are unequal because

$$
5\cdot2^2=20\ne24=3\cdot2^3.
$$

Thus $5/8\ne3/4$.

### Algorithm 5.4 (Equality test)

Given $(m_1,n_1)$ and $(m_2,n_2)$ representing $m_1/2^{n_1}$ and $m_2/2^{n_2}$:

1. Compute $A=m_1 2^{n_2}$.
2. Compute $B=m_2 2^{n_1}$.
3. Return equal exactly when $A=B$.

With arbitrary-precision binary integers, multiplication by $2^n$ is a bit shift. If the numerators have bit lengths at most $L$ and the exponents at most $N$, the arithmetic and comparison use $O(L+N)$ bit operations in the shift-based model, apart from memory allocation. No game-tree comparison is required.

## 6. Canonical normalization

A nonzero dyadic has a unique reduced presentation with odd numerator. If

$$
x=\frac{m}{2^n},
$$

and $m$ is even while $n>0$, divide $m$ by $2$ and decrease $n$ by $1$. Continue until $n=0$ or the numerator is odd. For zero, choose the canonical form $0/2^0$.

### Proposition 6.1 (Existence and uniqueness of reduced dyadic form)

Every dyadic rational has a representation $a/2^k$ such that either $a=0$ and $k=0$, or $a$ is odd. This representation is unique.

**Proof sketch.** Existence follows by repeatedly removing factors of $2$ from the numerator, a process that terminates because the exponent decreases. For uniqueness, suppose $a/2^k=b/2^\ell$ with odd nonzero $a,b$. Cross multiplication gives $a2^\ell=b2^k$. If $k<\ell$, the left side is even while the right side is odd after cancellation of $2^k$, a contradiction; similarly $\ell<k$ is impossible. Hence $k=\ell$, and then $a=b$. The zero case is fixed by convention. $\square$

### Algorithm 6.2 (Dyadic normalization)

Input an integer $m$ and nonnegative exponent $n$.

1. If $m=0$, return $(0,0)$.
2. While $n>0$ and $m$ is even, replace $(m,n)$ by $(m/2,n-1)$.
3. Return $(m,n)$.

The loop runs at most $n$ times and, more precisely, $\min(n,v_2(m))$ times, where $v_2(m)$ is the exponent of $2$ dividing $m$. On binary integers, trailing-zero counting can reduce normalization to essentially linear time in the bit length of $m$.

## 7. The obstruction to field structure

The dyadics are closed under addition, additive inverses, and multiplication. They therefore form a commutative ordered ring. They are not a field.

### Theorem 7.1 (Three has no dyadic inverse)

There is no $x\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ such that

$$
3x=1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Suppose $x=m/2^n$. Then $3m/2^n=1$, so

$$
3m=2^n.
$$

The left side is divisible by $3$. The right side is not: powers of $2$ are congruent to $1$ or $2$ modulo $3$, alternating with the parity of $n$. This contradiction proves that no such $x$ exists. $\square$

### Corollary 7.2 (The dyadic ring is not a field)

The ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is not a field.

**Proof sketch.** A field must provide a multiplicative inverse for every nonzero element. The nonzero element $3$ has none by Theorem 7.1. $\square$

### Corollary 7.3 (Finite birthday should not be called a subfield)

Any identification of finite-birthday surreal values with dyadic rationals yields a subring interpretation, not a subfield interpretation.

**Proof sketch.** The dyadic family contains $3$ but not its inverse $1/3$. Closure under all nonzero inverses therefore fails. $\square$

The issue is conceptual as well as algebraic. A cutoff

$$
B_\alpha=\{x:b(x)<\alpha\}
$$

records constructive availability. The ring generated by $B_\alpha$ records closure under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The field generated by $B_\alpha$ additionally includes inverses. These three sets can differ because arithmetic operations can increase birthdays and inversion can introduce values absent from the cutoff.

## 8. Algorithms and numerical applications

The proved criteria lead to direct computational procedures.

### 8.1. Exact dyadic arithmetic

Represent a dyadic by a pair $(m,n)$ denoting $m2^{-n}$. Addition uses a common binary scale, multiplication adds exponents, and normalization removes common factors of $2$. All operations remain in integer arithmetic and are exact. This is the mathematical basis of fixed-point binary computation.

### 8.2. Birthday computation for canonical units

For the canonical form $h_n$, no tree traversal is necessary once Theorem 3.1 is known: return $n+1$. Generating the first $N$ units produces the table

$$
(1,1),\left(\frac12,2\right),\ldots,
\left(2^{-(N-1)},N\right).
$$

The computation is $O(N)$ for the table, while a single birthday query is $O(1)$ in unit-cost arithmetic.

### 8.3. Binary-grid visualization

At resolution $n$, the dyadics in $[0,1]$ are

$$
\left\{\frac{k}{2^n}:0\le k\le2^n\right\}.
$$

Passing from level $n$ to $n+1$ retains every old point and inserts one midpoint into each old interval. This nested structure connects surreal construction with bisection, dyadic harmonic analysis, multiresolution geometry, and exact binary numerics.

### 8.4. Detecting invertibility inside the dyadic ring

A nonzero dyadic $m/2^n$ is a unit in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ exactly when its reduced numerator is $1$ or $-1$. Indeed, after normalization its reciprocal is dyadic only when no odd prime factor remains in the numerator. Therefore the units are precisely

$$
\{\pm2^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}.
$$

This generalizes the obstruction for $3$: every reduced odd numerator other than $\pm1$ prevents a dyadic inverse.

## 9. Applications and interpretation

### 9.1. Combinatorial game theory

Surreal arithmetic emerges from game positions, and birthdays measure the depth of recursive option trees. The exact formula $b(h_n)=n+1$ turns denominator scale into a transparent combinatorial invariant for canonical inverse powers of two.

### 9.2. Exact computation

Dyadic numbers are exactly the rationals with finite binary expansions. Their faithful surreal embedding ensures that calculations with pairs $(m,n)$ preserve equality exactly. The cross-product criterion avoids floating-point approximation and its rounding ambiguities.

### 9.3. Multiscale analysis

Dyadic intervals form a nested hierarchy. The sequence $h_n$ supplies the corresponding scale parameters, while strict decrease guarantees distinct scales. The birthday formula adds a constructive interpretation: each refinement level costs exactly one additional generation for the canonical unit.

### 9.4. Algebraic hierarchy

The failure of $1/3$ illustrates a general warning. Constructive rank and algebraic closure answer different questions. A hierarchy may contain many numbers and support substantial arithmetic without being a field at any fixed stage. Statements about higher birthday cutoffs must specify whether they concern raw cutoffs, generated rings, generated fields, or algebraic closures.

## 10. Boundary discipline: cutoffs, generated rings, and generated fields

The arithmetic obstruction above motivates three definitions that should accompany any birthday-indexed investigation. For an ordinal $\alpha$, let the **raw birthday cutoff** consist of values admitting a representative born before $\alpha$. Let the **generated ring** be the smallest subring of the surreal numbers containing that cutoff. Let the **generated field** be the smallest subfield containing it, whenever the ambient field operations under discussion are available. These constructions answer different questions.

The raw cutoff asks which values can be described with a bounded amount of genealogical depth. The generated ring asks what finite combinations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication can produce from those values. The generated field also permits division by every nonzero generated element. There are inclusions from the cutoff into its generated ring and from that ring into its generated field, but neither inclusion should be presumed to be equality.

The dyadic example makes the second gap explicit. All ordinary integers and canonical inverse powers of two occur at finite birthdays, and their ring combinations yield $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Yet field generation immediately includes $1/3$. Cross multiplication proves that no expression $m/2^n$ equals $1/3$, since such an equality would require $3m=2^n$. Thus field closure crosses the dyadic boundary.

There is also no general reason for a fixed raw cutoff to be closed under arithmetic. The birthday of a sum or product is controlled by recursive descriptions of its operands and can exceed either input birthday. Consequently, even when the union of all finite stages coincides with a familiar ring, an individual finite stage need not be a subring.

This three-level vocabulary prevents ambiguous statements such as “the numbers at stage $\alpha$ form a field.” A precise claim must identify both the birthday inequality, such as $b(x)<\alpha$, and the intended closure operation. It must then prove closure rather than infer it from the richness of the underlying collection. In the finite case, the missing inverse of $3$ supplies a minimal diagnostic: any proposed field description that excludes $1/3$ cannot be correct.

## 10. Limitations and future directions

The present results establish the canonical dyadic embedding and its arithmetic uniqueness, but they do not by themselves prove that every finite-birthday surreal value is dyadic. Completing that classification requires a “simplest dyadic in an interval” theorem: given finite sets of dyadic left and right options with every left option below every right option, one must identify the simplest intervening surreal as dyadic. Induction on finite birthday should then prove the forward classification.

A second direction is to enrich the canonical bijection with full ordered-ring structure once the needed multiplication theory is developed in the chosen surreal framework. The map should preserve addition and multiplication and identify its range as an ordered subring isomorphic to $\mathbb Z[1/2]$.

Third, the exact birthday of a general reduced noninteger dyadic $m/2^n$ should be determined. The denominator exponent alone is insufficient: the integer part and numerator affect the canonical construction. The theorem $b(h_n)=n+1$ is the fundamental special case.

Fourth, higher birthday claims need precise closure conventions. A set born before an ordinal need not itself be a ring or field, because operations may increase birthdays. Future formulations should separately name the birthday cutoff, the ring it generates, and the field it generates.

Finally, there is no smallest positive surreal infinitesimal. Whenever $x>0$ is infinitesimal, $x/2$ is a smaller positive infinitesimal. Therefore claims involving such an object must instead select a particular infinitesimal, for example $\omega^{-1}$. Even with that correction, a bounded-birthday class should not be identified without proof with a rational-function field such as $\mathbb R(\omega^{-1})$.

## 11. Conclusion

The canonical inverse powers of two form a precisely ordered and precisely dated family in the surreal hierarchy. The representative of $2^{-n}$ has birthday $n+1$; these values are positive, strictly decreasing, and distinct. No nonzero integer multiple of one of them vanishes. These facts establish a faithful embedding of $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ into the surreal numbers and reduce equality of canonical dyadic values to the cross-product identity

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

The same analysis identifies the boundary of the construction: $3$ has no inverse among the dyadics. The finite-birthday landscape is therefore naturally ring-like rather than field-like. This distinction supplies a sound foundation for future classification of finite-birthday surreals and for more careful investigation of the algebraic structures associated with transfinite birthday levels.

## A number born from a choice

Most number systems begin with objects and then add rules. The surreal numbers reverse that order. A surreal number is born from a choice between two collections of earlier numbers. It is written

$$
\{L\mid R\},
$$

where every member of the left set $L$ is smaller than every member of the right set $R$. The new number is the simplest number lying strictly between those options. This construction turns arithmetic into a family tree: each number has a birthday recording the stage at which its description first becomes available.

The first day is almost empty. With no options on either side, one obtains

$$
0=\{\,\mid\,\}.
$$

Once zero exists, the next stage produces

$$
1=\{0\mid\},\qquad -1=\{\mid 0\}.
$$

Then the gap between $0$ and $1$ yields

$$
\frac12=\{0\mid 1\}.
$$

The next rounds create halves of halves, odd numerators between neighboring fractions, and ever larger integers. This simple game of choosing a left and a right boundary eventually generates an enormous ordered number system containing the familiar real numbers, ordinal numbers, infinitely large quantities, and infinitesimals.

But the finite opening of this universe has a strikingly rigid arithmetic shape. It is governed not by arbitrary fractions, but by the **dyadic rationals**: numbers of the form

$$
\frac{m}{2^n},
$$

where $m$ is an integer and $n$ is a nonnegative integer. The arithmetic developed here explains why the powers of two are not an accident, why their canonical surreal representatives are distinct, and why this finite-birthday world is a ring rather than a field.

## The binary staircase

Begin with the canonical game for $1$ and repeatedly take the simplest number between $0$ and the preceding value. This creates

$$
1,\quad \frac12,\quad \frac14,\quad \frac18,\quad \ldots.
$$

The key birthday theorem says that the canonical representative of $2^{-n}$ has birthday exactly $n+1$. Thus $1=2^0$ appears at birthday $1$, $1/2$ at birthday $2$, $1/4$ at birthday $3$, and so on.

This result says two things at once. First, every inverse power of two appears after finitely many stages. Second, no fixed finite stage contains them all: their birthdays are unbounded among the natural numbers. The approach to zero is therefore also a journey deeper into the construction.

These values behave exactly as their ordinary fractional notation suggests. Every $2^{-n}$ is positive, and the sequence is strictly decreasing:

$$
2^{-(n+1)}<2^{-n}.
$$

Consequently, two canonical inverse powers of two are equal if and only if their exponents agree. The hierarchy does not accidentally collapse $1/4$ and $1/8$, for example; order keeps every rung of the binary staircase separate.

There is another essential cancellation fact. If $m$ is an integer, then

$$
m\,2^{-n}=0
$$

holds if and only if $m=0$. A nonzero integer cannot annihilate a positive inverse power of two. This elementary-looking statement is the hinge on which uniqueness turns.

## Fractions that cannot disguise themselves

A dyadic number can have more than one written form. For instance,

$$
\frac12=\frac24=\frac48.
$$

So the right uniqueness statement cannot require identical numerators and denominators. Instead, it uses the familiar rule of cross multiplication.

For integers $m_1,m_2$ and nonnegative integers $n_1,n_2$, the corresponding surreal dyadics satisfy

$$
m_1 2^{-n_1}=m_2 2^{-n_2}
$$

if and only if

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

This is the **Cross-Multiplication Theorem for Dyadic Surreals**. It provides a complete test for equality using integer arithmetic alone. As an example,

$$
\frac{6}{2^4}=\frac{3}{2^3}
$$

because $6\cdot 2^3=3\cdot 2^4=48$. By contrast,

$$
\frac{5}{2^3}\ne\frac{3}{2^2}
$$

because $5\cdot 2^2=20$ while $3\cdot 2^3=24$.

This criterion proves that the canonical map from the localized ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ into the surreal numbers is injective. Here $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ means the integers with powers of two made invertible; concretely, it is precisely the set of fractions $m/2^n$. Injectivity means that no two genuinely different dyadic rationals become the same surreal number. The image is therefore a faithful copy of dyadic arithmetic inside the surreal universe.

There is a practical lesson here. Equality in a recursively generated world may look like a question about game trees, but for this entire family it reduces to a single multiplication test in the integers. The elaborate genealogy of a number and its ordinary arithmetic value agree perfectly.

## A ring, not a field

It is tempting to call every rich collection of numbers a field. The dyadic rationals are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication:

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
 =\frac{a2^n+b2^m}{2^{m+n}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}\frac{b}{2^n}=\frac{ab}{2^{m+n}}.
$$

They also contain $0$ and $1$. These properties make them a commutative ring. Yet division exposes a boundary. The number $3$ has no multiplicative inverse in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some dyadic $m/2^n$ were an inverse of $3$. Then

$$
3\frac{m}{2^n}=1,
$$

so

$$
3m=2^n.
$$

The left side is divisible by $3$, whereas no power of $2$ is divisible by $3$. This is impossible. Hence $1/3$ is not dyadic.

This obstruction corrects a subtle but important misconception about birthdays. The numbers born at finite stages are naturally associated with the dyadic **subring**, not a subfield. Closing that collection under multiplicative inverses would immediately force the inclusion of $1/3$, which does not have a finite birthday in the canonical surreal hierarchy.

The distinction matters far beyond terminology. A birthday cutoff describes when objects are constructed. A ring closure describes which objects arithmetic operations generate. A field closure additionally demands every nonzero inverse. These are different processes, and they need not preserve the same boundary.

## Why powers of two rule the finite days

The appearance of dyadics reflects a universal fact about repeatedly selecting simplest midpoints. Given neighboring dyadic boundaries, the simplest point inserted between them refines the denominator by a factor of two. Binary subdivision is built into the construction:

$$
0,1
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
0,\frac12,1
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,1.
$$

This is the same geometry behind binary search, bisection algorithms, digital fixed-point arithmetic, and subdivision meshes in computer graphics. A finite binary word records a finite route through successive left-right choices. Correspondingly, a dyadic fraction is exactly a rational number with a terminating binary expansion.

For example,

$$
\frac{13}{16}=0.1101_2.
$$

Its denominator records four levels of binary resolution. Surreal birthdays add a genealogical interpretation: denominator depth measures part of the history required to isolate the number, though for general dyadics the exact birthday also depends on the integer part and reduction of the fraction.

This makes dyadic surreals useful as a conceptual bridge. In numerical computation, dyadic fractions are the exactly representable finite binary values. In harmonic analysis, dyadic intervals organize functions by scale. In combinatorial game theory, birthdays organize numbers by constructive complexity. The same powers of two describe precision, scale, and ancestry.

## The horizon at day $\omega$

All finite birthdays lie before the first infinite ordinal $\omega$. The sequence $2^{-n}$ demonstrates what happens near that horizon: each term is born finitely, but there is no final finite day on which the entire sequence appears. The union of all finite stages contains every dyadic fraction, while remaining arithmetically incomplete as a field.

The surreal numbers show how a vast arithmetic universe can grow from an austere rule: choose earlier values on the left and right, then create the simplest number between them. ## Abstract

Surreal numbers are recursively generated from cuts between previously constructed numbers, and their birthdays measure the stages at which representatives become available. This paper isolates the canonical dyadic fragment of that hierarchy. We prove that the canonical surreal representative of $2^{-n}$ has birthday exactly $n+1$, that these representatives are positive and strictly decreasing, and that a multiple $m2^{-n}$ vanishes only for $m=0$. We then establish that the canonical map from the localization $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ into the surreal numbers is injective. As a consequence, equality of two canonical dyadic surreal values is equivalent to the integer cross-product identity

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

Finally, we prove that $3$ has no inverse in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Thus the finite-birthday layer is naturally associated with the dyadic subring, not a subfield. The results clarify the distinction among birthday cutoffs, algebraic closures, and fields generated by birthday-bounded classes, while providing exact algorithms for equality, normalization, arithmetic, and birthday computation for canonical inverse powers of two.

## 1. Introduction

The surreal numbers arise from a recursive construction in which a new number is specified by previously available left and right options. A form

$$
x=\{L\mid R\}
$$

is valid when every $\ell\in L$ is less than every $r\in R$; its value is the simplest surreal number strictly between all left and right options. Starting from the empty cut, this process creates $0$, then the integers $\pm1$, then fractions such as $1/2$, and eventually a proper class encompassing the real numbers, ordinals, infinitesimals, and infinitely large quantities.

The recursive stages are measured by **birthdays**. The birthday of a form is one greater than the supremum of the birthdays of its options, with the empty form assigned birthday $0$. Birthday therefore records constructive depth rather than ordinary magnitude. An enormous integer and a tiny positive fraction can both have finite birthdays, but their exact dates reflect different genealogies.

The finite stages have long suggested a binary pattern. Repeatedly choosing the simplest value between $0$ and a previously created positive value yields

$$
1,\frac12,\frac14,\frac18,\ldots.
$$

More generally, finite binary subdivision produces numbers $m/2^n$. These are the dyadic rationals, algebraically described as the localization $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ obtained from $\mathbb Z$ by inverting $2$.

This paper develops the exact arithmetic facts required to identify the canonical dyadic values faithfully inside the surreal numbers. The principal issue is injectivity: distinct elements of $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ must not collapse to the same surreal value. Once injectivity is known, equality reduces to cross multiplication, exactly as for ordinary fractions.

A second objective is corrective. The dyadic rationals are sometimes described informally as a field, or the finite-birthday surreals as a subfield. This is false. Although $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is a commutative ordered ring, it does not contain $1/3$. We give an elementary obstruction proving that $3$ has no multiplicative inverse. Therefore finite birthdays, ring generation, and field generation must be distinguished.

## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1. Surreal forms and birthdays

A **surreal form** is a pair $\{L\mid R\}$ of sets of earlier forms satisfying $\ell<r$ for every $\ell\in L$ and $r\in R$. Two different forms may represent the same surreal number. The birthday belongs to a form and is recursively defined by

$$
b\bigl(\{L\mid R\}\bigr)
=
\sup\{b(y)+1:y\in L\cup R\}.
$$

For finite game trees, this is simply one plus the maximum birthday among all options. In particular,

$$
0=\{\mid\},\qquad b(0)=0,
$$

and

$$
1=\{0\mid\},\qquad b(1)=1.
$$

The distinction between a form and its value is important. Our birthday statements concern canonical recursively defined forms, while arithmetic statements concern their surreal values.

### 2.2. Canonical inverse powers of two

Define canonical forms $h_n$ recursively by

$$
h_0=1,
\qquad
h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}.
$$

The value of $h_n$ is $2^{-n}$. Thus

$$
h_0=1,
\quad h_1=\frac12,
\quad h_2=\frac14,
\quad h_3=\frac18.
$$

The cut description expresses $h_{n+1}$ as the simplest surreal number strictly between $0$ and $h_n$.

### 2.3. Dyadic rationals as a localization

The **dyadic rationals** form the ring

$$
D=\mathbb Z[1/2]
 =\left\{\frac{m}{2^n}:m\in\mathbb Z,\ n\in\mathbb N\right\}.
$$

Two presentations represent the same element precisely when

$$
\frac{m_1}{2^{n_1}}=\frac{m_2}{2^{n_2}}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

Addition and multiplication are given by

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{a2^n+b2^m}{2^{m+n}},
$$

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{ab}{2^{m+n}}.
$$

A more economical addition algorithm first raises both values only to the common exponent $k=\max(m,n)$:

$$
\frac{a}{2^m}+\frac{b}{2^n}
=
\frac{a2^{k-m}+b2^{k-n}}{2^k}.
$$

The canonical map into the surreal numbers is

$$
\iota:D\longrightarrow \mathbf{No},
\qquad
\iota\left(\frac{m}{2^n}\right)=m h_n=m2^{-n}.
$$

The central task is to show that this formula is independent of presentation and that $\iota$ is injective.

## 3. Birthday and order structure

### Theorem 3.1 (Exact birthday of a canonical dyadic unit)

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the canonical form $h_n$ representing $2^{-n}$ has birthday

$$
b(h_n)=n+1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The argument is induction on $n$. The base form $h_0=1=\{0\mid\}$ has birthday $1$. For the induction step, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$. Its options have birthdays $0$ and $n+1$, so the recursive birthday rule gives

$$
b(h_{n+1})=1+\max(0,n+1)=n+2.
$$

This is the required formula with $n$ replaced by $n+1$. $\square$

### Corollary 3.2 (Finite but unbounded birthdays)

Every canonical inverse power $2^{-n}$ has a finite-birthday representative, but their birthdays are unbounded among the finite ordinals.

**Proof sketch.** Finiteness follows from $b(h_n)=n+1$. Given any finite bound $N$, choosing $n\ge N$ yields $b(h_n)=n+1>N$. $\square$

### Theorem 3.3 (Positivity)

For every $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
0<h_n.
$$

**Proof sketch.** The base case $h_0=1$ is positive. Recursively, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$ is defined as a number strictly to the right of its left option $0$. Hence it is positive. $\square$

### Theorem 3.4 (Strict decrease)

The sequence $n\mapsto h_n$ is strictly decreasing. Equivalently,

$$
h_{n+1}<h_n
$$

for every $n$, and if $m<n$ then $h_n<h_m$.

**Proof sketch.** By construction, $h_{n+1}=\{0\mid h_n\}$ lies strictly below its right option $h_n$. Iterating this adjacent inequality proves strict antitonicity. $\square$

### Corollary 3.5 (Distinct exponents give distinct units)

For $m,n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
h_m=h_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m=n.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Equality follows immediately when $m=n$. Conversely, a strictly decreasing sequence is injective, so equal values force equal indices. $\square$

These results exhibit a direct relation between genealogy and order. As birthday increases along this family, value decreases toward zero. The family has no least positive member because $h_{n+1}$ is always a smaller positive member than $h_n$.

## 4. Cancellation and faithful embedding

### Lemma 4.1 (No nontrivial integer annihilator)

For every $m\in\mathbb Z$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$
mh_n=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m=0.
$$

**Proof sketch.** If $m=0$, the equality is immediate. Conversely, $h_n>0$, hence $h_n\ne0$. The ordered additive group of surreal numbers is torsion-free: a positive integer multiple of a positive value is positive, while a negative integer multiple is negative. Therefore a nonzero integer multiple of $h_n$ cannot vanish. $\square$

The next result is the main arithmetic statement.

### Theorem 4.2 (Injectivity of the canonical dyadic map)

The map

$$
\iota:\mathbb Z[1/2]\longrightarrow\mathbf{No},
\qquad
\iota(m/2^n)=mh_n,
$$

is injective.

**Proof sketch.** Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ and suppose $\iota(x)=\iota(y)$. Choose presentations

$$
x=\frac{a}{2^r},\qquad y=\frac{b}{2^s}.
$$

Raise both to the common denominator $2^{r+s}$:

$$
x=\frac{a2^s}{2^{r+s}},
\qquad
 y=\frac{b2^r}{2^{r+s}}.
$$

Their surreal images are therefore integer multiples of the same positive unit $h_{r+s}$. Equality gives

$$
(a2^s-b2^r)h_{r+s}=0.
$$

By Lemma 4.1, $a2^s-b2^r=0$. Hence the two fractions are equal in the localization, so $x=y$. $\square$

### Corollary 4.3 (Canonical equivalence with the dyadic image)

The dyadic rational ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is in canonical bijection with its image in the surreal numbers.

**Proof sketch.** Any map is surjective onto its image. Combining this fact with Theorem 4.2 gives a bijection. $\square$

This equivalence is an exact identification at the level of values: each dyadic rational has one surreal value, and each surreal value in the image has one dyadic rational antecedent. The theorem does not claim that all surreal numbers are dyadic, nor by itself classify every finite-birthday form.

## 5. Equality by cross multiplication

### Theorem 5.1 (Cross-Multiplication Theorem)

For all $m_1,m_2\in\mathbb Z$ and $n_1,n_2\in\mathbb N$,

$$
m_1h_{n_1}=m_2h_{n_2}
$$

if and only if

$$
m_1 2^{n_2}=m_2 2^{n_1}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Regard the two sides as the images under $\iota$ of $m_1/2^{n_1}$ and $m_2/2^{n_2}$. Injectivity of $\iota$ converts equality of surreal values into equality in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Equality of localized fractions is exactly the displayed cross-product identity. Conversely, the cross-product identity proves equality of fractions, and applying $\iota$ gives equality of their surreal values. $\square$

### Example 5.2

The values $6h_4$ and $3h_3$ are equal because

$$
6\cdot2^3=48=3\cdot2^4.
$$

Both represent $3/8$.

### Example 5.3

The values $5h_3$ and $3h_2$ are unequal because

$$
5\cdot2^2=20\ne24=3\cdot2^3.
$$

Thus $5/8\ne3/4$.

### Algorithm 5.4 (Equality test)

Given $(m_1,n_1)$ and $(m_2,n_2)$ representing $m_1/2^{n_1}$ and $m_2/2^{n_2}$:

1. Compute $A=m_1 2^{n_2}$.
2. Compute $B=m_2 2^{n_1}$.
3. Return equal exactly when $A=B$.

With arbitrary-precision binary integers, multiplication by $2^n$ is a bit shift. If the numerators have bit lengths at most $L$ and the exponents at most $N$, the arithmetic and comparison use $O(L+N)$ bit operations in the shift-based model, apart from memory allocation. No game-tree comparison is required.

## 6. Canonical normalization

A nonzero dyadic has a unique reduced presentation with odd numerator. If

$$
x=\frac{m}{2^n},
$$

and $m$ is even while $n>0$, divide $m$ by $2$ and decrease $n$ by $1$. Continue until $n=0$ or the numerator is odd. For zero, choose the canonical form $0/2^0$.

### Proposition 6.1 (Existence and uniqueness of reduced dyadic form)

Every dyadic rational has a representation $a/2^k$ such that either $a=0$ and $k=0$, or $a$ is odd. This representation is unique.

**Proof sketch.** Existence follows by repeatedly removing factors of $2$ from the numerator, a process that terminates because the exponent decreases. For uniqueness, suppose $a/2^k=b/2^\ell$ with odd nonzero $a,b$. Cross multiplication gives $a2^\ell=b2^k$. If $k<\ell$, the left side is even while the right side is odd after cancellation of $2^k$, a contradiction; similarly $\ell<k$ is impossible. Hence $k=\ell$, and then $a=b$. The zero case is fixed by convention. $\square$

### Algorithm 6.2 (Dyadic normalization)

Input an integer $m$ and nonnegative exponent $n$.

1. If $m=0$, return $(0,0)$.
2. While $n>0$ and $m$ is even, replace $(m,n)$ by $(m/2,n-1)$.
3. Return $(m,n)$.

The loop runs at most $n$ times and, more precisely, $\min(n,v_2(m))$ times, where $v_2(m)$ is the exponent of $2$ dividing $m$. On binary integers, trailing-zero counting can reduce normalization to essentially linear time in the bit length of $m$.

## 7. The obstruction to field structure

The dyadics are closed under addition, additive inverses, and multiplication. They therefore form a commutative ordered ring. They are not a field.

### Theorem 7.1 (Three has no dyadic inverse)

There is no $x\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ such that

$$
3x=1.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Suppose $x=m/2^n$. Then $3m/2^n=1$, so

$$
3m=2^n.
$$

The left side is divisible by $3$. The right side is not: powers of $2$ are congruent to $1$ or $2$ modulo $3$, alternating with the parity of $n$. This contradiction proves that no such $x$ exists. $\square$

### Corollary 7.2 (The dyadic ring is not a field)

The ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ is not a field.

**Proof sketch.** A field must provide a multiplicative inverse for every nonzero element. The nonzero element $3$ has none by Theorem 7.1. $\square$

### Corollary 7.3 (Finite birthday should not be called a subfield)

Any identification of finite-birthday surreal values with dyadic rationals yields a subring interpretation, not a subfield interpretation.

**Proof sketch.** The dyadic family contains $3$ but not its inverse $1/3$. Closure under all nonzero inverses therefore fails. $\square$

The issue is conceptual as well as algebraic. A cutoff

$$
B_\alpha=\{x:b(x)<\alpha\}
$$

records constructive availability. The ring generated by $B_\alpha$ records closure under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The field generated by $B_\alpha$ additionally includes inverses. These three sets can differ because arithmetic operations can increase birthdays and inversion can introduce values absent from the cutoff.

## 8. Algorithms and numerical applications

The proved criteria lead to direct computational procedures.

### 8.1. Exact dyadic arithmetic

Represent a dyadic by a pair $(m,n)$ denoting $m2^{-n}$. Addition uses a common binary scale, multiplication adds exponents, and normalization removes common factors of $2$. All operations remain in integer arithmetic and are exact. This is the mathematical basis of fixed-point binary computation.

### 8.2. Birthday computation for canonical units

For the canonical form $h_n$, no tree traversal is necessary once Theorem 3.1 is known: return $n+1$. Generating the first $N$ units produces the table

$$
(1,1),\left(\frac12,2\right),\ldots,
\left(2^{-(N-1)},N\right).
$$

The computation is $O(N)$ for the table, while a single birthday query is $O(1)$ in unit-cost arithmetic.

### 8.3. Binary-grid visualization

At resolution $n$, the dyadics in $[0,1]$ are

$$
\left\{\frac{k}{2^n}:0\le k\le2^n\right\}.
$$

Passing from level $n$ to $n+1$ retains every old point and inserts one midpoint into each old interval. This nested structure connects surreal construction with bisection, dyadic harmonic analysis, multiresolution geometry, and exact binary numerics.

### 8.4. Detecting invertibility inside the dyadic ring

A nonzero dyadic $m/2^n$ is a unit in $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ exactly when its reduced numerator is $1$ or $-1$. Indeed, after normalization its reciprocal is dyadic only when no odd prime factor remains in the numerator. Therefore the units are precisely

$$
\{\pm2^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}.
$$

This generalizes the obstruction for $3$: every reduced odd numerator other than $\pm1$ prevents a dyadic inverse.

## 9. Applications and interpretation

### 9.1. Combinatorial game theory

Surreal arithmetic emerges from game positions, and birthdays measure the depth of recursive option trees. The exact formula $b(h_n)=n+1$ turns denominator scale into a transparent combinatorial invariant for canonical inverse powers of two.

### 9.2. Exact computation

Dyadic numbers are exactly the rationals with finite binary expansions. Their faithful surreal embedding ensures that calculations with pairs $(m,n)$ preserve equality exactly. The cross-product criterion avoids floating-point approximation and its rounding ambiguities.

### 9.3. Multiscale analysis

Dyadic intervals form a nested hierarchy. The sequence $h_n$ supplies the corresponding scale parameters, while strict decrease guarantees distinct scales. The birthday formula adds a constructive interpretation: each refinement level costs exactly one additional generation for the canonical unit.

### 9.4. Algebraic hierarchy

The failure of $1/3$ illustrates a general warning. Constructive rank and algebraic closure answer different questions. A hierarchy may contain many numbers and support substantial arithmetic without being a field at any fixed stage. Statements about higher birthday cutoffs must specify whether they concern raw cutoffs, generated rings, generated fields, or algebraic closures.

## 10. Boundary discipline: cutoffs, generated rings, and generated fields

The arithmetic obstruction above motivates three definitions that should accompany any birthday-indexed investigation. For an ordinal $\alpha$, let the **raw birthday cutoff** consist of values admitting a representative born before $\alpha$. Let the **generated ring** be the smallest subring of the surreal numbers containing that cutoff. Let the **generated field** be the smallest subfield containing it, whenever the ambient field operations under discussion are available. These constructions answer different questions.

The raw cutoff asks which values can be described with a bounded amount of genealogical depth. The generated ring asks what finite combinations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication can produce from those values. The generated field also permits division by every nonzero generated element. There are inclusions from the cutoff into its generated ring and from that ring into its generated field, but neither inclusion should be presumed to be equality.

The dyadic example makes the second gap explicit. All ordinary integers and canonical inverse powers of two occur at finite birthdays, and their ring combinations yield $\mathbb Z[1/2]$. Yet field generation immediately includes $1/3$. Cross multiplication proves that no expression $m/2^n$ equals $1/3$, since such an equality would require $3m=2^n$. Thus field closure crosses the dyadic boundary.

There is also no general reason for a fixed raw cutoff to be closed under arithmetic. The birthday of a sum or product is controlled by recursive descriptions of its operands and can exceed either input birthday. Consequently, even when the union of all finite stages coincides with a familiar ring, an individual finite stage need not be a subring.

This three-level vocabulary prevents ambiguous statements such as “the numbers at stage $\alpha$ form a field.” A precise claim must identify both the birthday inequality, such as $b(x)<\alpha$, and the intended closure operation. It must then prove closure rather than infer it from the richness of the underlying collection. In the finite case, the missing inverse of $3$ supplies a minimal diagnostic: any proposed field description that excludes $1/3$ cannot be correct.

## 10. Limitations and future directions

The present results establish the canonical dyadic embedding and its arithmetic uniqueness, but they do not by themselves prove that every finite-birthday surreal value is dyadic. Completing that classification requires a “simplest dyadic in an interval” theorem: given finite sets of dyadic left and right options with every left option below every right option, one must identify the simplest intervening surreal as dyadic. Induction on finite birthday should then prove the forward classification.
